title: Domain 4: Network Security
description: Original practice questions for domain 4 of the CompTIA Network+ N10-009 objectives, written from the published objectives and vendor documentation.

questions.prompt: Which three properties make up the security triad?

options.text: Confidentiality, integrity, availability
Confidentiality, identity, authorisation
Control, integrity, assurance
Compliance, integrity, availability

questions.explanation: The triad is confidentiality, integrity and availability, and it is worth holding because most controls trade one against another. Identity and authorisation are important concepts that sit alongside the triad rather than inside it. Control and assurance are process words rather than properties of information. Compliance is an obligation that may require all three and is not one of them.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a vulnerability and a threat?

options.text: A vulnerability is a weakness; a threat is what might exploit it
A vulnerability is external; a threat is internal
A vulnerability is theoretical; a threat is confirmed
A vulnerability applies to software and a threat to people

questions.explanation: A weakness exists whether or not anybody is interested in it, and a threat is the actor or event that could act on it, which is why risk needs both together with the impact. Internal against external describes where something originates rather than which word applies. Both can be theoretical or confirmed. Neither is restricted to software or to people, which is exactly why the vocabulary is worth being precise about.

questions.prompt: Why is availability treated as a security property rather than an operations one?

options.text: An attack that makes a system unusable has caused a security failure
Availability is easier to measure than the other two properties
Regulators require availability reporting more often than confidentiality
Availability failures are always caused by attackers

questions.explanation: Denying access to information is a way of harming the people who depend on it, so an outage caused deliberately is a security incident even though nothing was read or altered. Ease of measurement is a practical convenience and not the reason it is in the triad. Regulatory attention varies and does not define the concept. Most availability failures have nothing to do with attackers, which is precisely why the property matters to both disciplines.

questions.prompt: Why do secure protocols use both asymmetric and symmetric encryption?

options.text: Asymmetric exchanges a key; symmetric is fast enough for the data
Asymmetric is stronger and symmetric provides a fallback
Asymmetric protects the payload and symmetric protects the headers
Asymmetric is used by servers and symmetric by clients

questions.explanation: Public key operations are expensive, so they are used to authenticate and to agree a shared key, and the bulk data is then protected with a symmetric cipher that is far faster. Strength is not the axis, since both can be configured to appropriate strength. Neither is assigned to headers or payloads. Both ends use both, so splitting them by role misdescribes the exchange.

questions.prompt: What does a certificate actually assert?

options.text: That a named identity holds a particular public key
That the named server is free of vulnerabilities
That traffic to the named server is encrypted
That the named organisation is trustworthy

questions.explanation: A certificate binds an identity to a public key and is signed by an authority somebody has chosen to trust, which is the entire claim. It says nothing about the security of the host, which can be certified and thoroughly compromised. It does not itself encrypt anything; it enables a key exchange that leads to encryption. Trustworthiness of the organisation is not verified by the technical process, and the amount of checking behind a certificate varies by type.

questions.prompt: A browser reports a certificate error and the certificate is valid and unexpired. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The name on the certificate does not match the name requested
The certificate uses an outdated key length
The server is using symmetric encryption only
The client's clock is set correctly but in a different time zone

questions.explanation: A name mismatch is the most common certificate error after expiry, and it happens whenever a site is reached by an address or an alternative name the certificate does not cover. Key length problems produce a different message and are rarer on current infrastructure. Symmetric encryption alone would break the handshake rather than produce a certificate error. Time zones are handled by comparing absolute times, so a correct clock in another zone is not a problem; a wrong clock is.

questions.prompt: What does a padlock in a browser prove?

options.text: The connection is encrypted to whoever presented a valid certificate
The site is operated by a legitimate business
The content of the site has been checked for malicious code
The site cannot record anything about the visitor

questions.explanation: It confirms the connection is encrypted and the certificate validates for the name in the address bar, which says who you are talking to rather than whether they deserve it. Legitimacy of the business is not established, since certificates are cheap and quick for anybody who controls a name. Content is not inspected by anybody in the process. The site can record whatever it likes, and encryption protects the traffic rather than the visitor's privacy from the site itself.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?

options.text: Authentication establishes who you are; authorisation what you may do
Authentication establishes what you may do; authorisation who you are
Authentication applies to users and authorisation to devices
Authentication is performed once and authorisation continuously

questions.explanation: Proving identity and deciding permissions are two separate questions, and conflating them is the source of a great many access problems, since a correctly authenticated user can still be denied. Reversing them is the common error. Both apply to users and to devices alike. Both can be evaluated repeatedly, and continuous evaluation of both is a feature of zero trust designs.

questions.prompt: Which combination is genuinely multi-factor?

options.text: A password and a code from a hardware token
A password and a security question
A password and a personal identification number
A fingerprint and a facial scan

questions.explanation: A password is something you know and a hardware token is something you have, so the two are different factors and compromising one does not yield the other. A security question is another thing you know, so it adds a second secret rather than a second factor. A personal identification number is also something you know. A fingerprint and a face are both something you are, so despite being two checks they are one factor.

questions.prompt: Which service is designed to separate authentication from authorisation and encrypt the whole exchange?

options.text: TACACS+
RADIUS
LDAP
Kerberos

questions.explanation: TACACS+ separates authentication, authorisation and accounting into distinct exchanges and encrypts the whole payload, which is why it is favoured for administrative access to devices. RADIUS combines authentication and authorisation and encrypts only the password field, which is the distinction worth memorising. LDAP is a directory access protocol rather than an authentication service, although it is frequently the directory behind one. Kerberos is a ticket-based authentication protocol with a different design again.

questions.prompt: Why are permissions assigned to roles rather than to individuals?

options.text: A person changing job means changing one assignment rather than many
Roles allow permissions to be granted without approval
Individual permissions cannot be audited
Roles remove the need to review access periodically

questions.explanation: Attaching permissions to a role and people to roles means a change of job is one change, which is what stops permissions accumulating as people move around. Approval is still required and roles make what is being approved clearer. Individual permissions can be audited and doing so is far more work. Periodic review is still necessary, and roles make it tractable rather than unnecessary.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of an account that remains active after somebody leaves?

options.text: Credentials exist that nobody is watching or expecting to be used
The licence for that account continues to be charged
The directory becomes larger and slower to search
Password policies cannot be enforced on inactive accounts

questions.explanation: An account nobody expects to be used is one whose misuse nobody will notice, and it may hold access that was appropriate for a job that no longer exists. Licence cost is a real annoyance and is not a security risk. Directory size is not a meaningful problem at any normal scale. Password policies apply to accounts regardless of whether anybody is using them.

questions.prompt: Why is physical access treated as its own security domain?

options.text: Somebody at the equipment can bypass most logical controls
Physical controls are cheaper than logical ones
Logical controls cannot be applied to network equipment
Physical attacks are more common than remote ones

questions.explanation: Console access, removing a disk, resetting a device or plugging into a spare port all bypass carefully built logical controls, which is why physical security underpins the rest. Cost varies enormously and is not the reason. Logical controls apply to network equipment and are exactly what physical access undermines. Remote attacks are far more common, and the point is that a physical one is more thorough rather than more frequent.

questions.prompt: What is tailgating?

options.text: Following an authorised person through a controlled door
Watching somebody enter a code or password
Sending a message that appears to come from a colleague
Leaving a device where somebody will pick it up and connect it

questions.explanation: Tailgating is entering behind somebody who legitimately opened the door, which defeats a badge reader without attacking it, and it succeeds because most people will not challenge somebody carrying a box. Watching credentials being entered is shoulder surfing. A message appearing to come from a colleague is a phishing or impersonation technique. Leaving a device to be picked up is baiting, usually with removable media.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a honeypot?

options.text: To attract activity that is unambiguously unauthorised and observe it
To absorb attack traffic so production systems stay available
To hold decoy data that is worthless if stolen
To slow an attacker by responding very slowly

questions.explanation: Nothing legitimate has any reason to touch a honeypot, so any interaction with it is a high-confidence signal, which is the value: alerts without the false positives that plague other detection. Absorbing attack traffic is what mitigation services do at far greater scale. Decoy data is a related idea and is not the defining purpose. Deliberate slowness describes a tarpit, which is a different technique.

questions.prompt: Why does regulation reach network design rather than stopping at applications?

options.text: Where data travels and who can reach it are network decisions
Regulators certify network equipment before it may be used
Applications are exempt from most data protection rules
Network devices store regulated data by default

questions.explanation: Segmentation, routing, encryption in transit and access control are all network decisions, and they determine which systems can reach regulated data and where that data crosses borders. Regulators do not certify equipment for general use. Applications are very much in scope and often the primary focus. Network devices generally do not store regulated data, and their configurations and logs are still in scope.

questions.prompt: What does data locality constrain?

options.text: Where data may be stored and processed geographically
Which applications may read a given data set
How long data must be retained before deletion
Which encryption algorithms may be used on data

questions.explanation: Locality rules say data about certain people or activities must stay within defined jurisdictions, which affects where you may place services and how traffic may be routed. Application access is governed by authorisation. Retention periods are a separate requirement that frequently appears in the same regulations. Approved algorithms are a cryptographic requirement rather than a geographic one.

questions.prompt: What does network segmentation actually enforce?

options.text: A policy about which segments may reach which, applied at a boundary
Physical separation between groups of devices
Different addressing schemes for different departments
Encryption of traffic between segments

questions.explanation: Segmentation is a reachability policy enforced at a boundary device, which is why a segmented device can still reach what it is supposed to and nothing else. Physical separation is one way to implement it and is not what the term means, since most segmentation is logical. Different addressing follows from segmentation and does not create it, as two subnets with no filtering between them are routed together freely. Encryption between segments is a separate control.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of flooding a switch with fabricated source addresses?

options.text: The table fills and unknown traffic is flooded everywhere
The switch reboots once its forwarding table is exhausted
The switch blocks the port the fabricated traffic arrived on
The switch stops learning entirely and forwards nothing at all

questions.explanation: Once the table is full the switch cannot learn new entries, so traffic for unknown destinations is flooded out of every port and becomes visible to the attacker, which is the goal. Switches do not reboot on a full table. Blocking the port is what port security does when configured and is a defence rather than the default behaviour. Forwarding nothing would be an outage, and flooding everything is worse from a confidentiality point of view.

questions.prompt: What does an attacker achieve by poisoning address resolution on a segment?

options.text: Traffic between two hosts is sent through the attacker's machine
Hosts on the segment lose their addresses and cannot communicate
The switch's forwarding table is cleared
The default gateway stops routing for the segment

questions.explanation: Convincing hosts that the attacker owns an address they need puts the attacker in the path, which is what makes it a machine in the middle attack. Loss of addresses would be a denial of service and is a possible side effect rather than the objective. The switch's table is not cleared, and it continues to forward frames correctly to the addresses it has learned. The gateway keeps routing; what changes is who the hosts send to.

questions.prompt: Which configuration weakness enables VLAN hopping?

options.text: A port that negotiates trunking, or a shared untagged VLAN
A port with port security enabled and no maximum configured
A trunk carrying rather more VLANs than it actually needs
An access port that carries a static address table entry

questions.explanation: The two classic routes are a port that will negotiate into a trunk and a design where the untagged VLAN on a trunk is also a user VLAN, which makes double tagging possible. Port security without a maximum is a misconfiguration that limits nothing and does not create hopping. A trunk carrying unnecessary VLANs is untidy and increases exposure without providing the mechanism. A static address entry on an access port restricts rather than enables.

questions.prompt: Why is a distributed denial of service attack difficult to defend against at the target?

options.text: It arrives from many sources and can saturate the link
The traffic is encrypted and therefore cannot be inspected
The traffic uses protocols that cannot be blocked anywhere
The traffic originates inside the target's own network

questions.explanation: If the access link is full, filtering at the far end of it changes nothing, because the traffic has already consumed the capacity, which is why mitigation happens upstream. Encryption is not what makes it hard, and much attack traffic is not encrypted. Any protocol can be blocked; the difficulty is that blocking it at the wrong place is too late. Distributed attacks come from outside by definition, and the many-source aspect is what defeats simple source blocking.

questions.prompt: A rogue DHCP server appears on a network. What is the immediate effect on clients?

options.text: Some clients accept its offer and get the settings it chooses
All clients lose their addresses at once
The legitimate server stops responding to requests
Clients receive two addresses and use both

questions.explanation: A client takes the first acceptable offer, so whichever server answers first wins for that client, which means some clients get a gateway and resolver of the attacker's choosing while others are unaffected. Existing leases are unaffected until renewal, so nothing happens to everybody at once. The legitimate server carries on answering. A client accepts one offer rather than two.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes spear phishing from phishing?

options.text: It is targeted at a specific person using details about them
It is delivered by telephone rather than by email
It uses a malicious attachment rather than a link
It targets an organisation rather than an individual

questions.explanation: Spear phishing is tailored using knowledge of the target, which is what makes it far more convincing and much harder to filter. Telephone delivery is vishing. The choice between attachment and link is a delivery detail present in both. Targeting an organisation broadly is ordinary phishing, and the narrowing to one person is the distinction.

questions.prompt: Why is an on-path attack often invisible to the two parties?

options.text: Traffic still arrives correctly, so nothing appears to fail
The attacker slows traffic so much that users blame the network
The attacker blocks all logging on both endpoints
Both parties receive a warning that they usually ignore

questions.explanation: The attacker forwards traffic on, so the conversation works and neither side has a symptom to report, which is exactly what makes it worth doing rather than simply blocking. Noticeable slowness would draw attention and defeat the purpose. The attacker cannot generally reach the endpoints' logging. Warnings appear where certificate validation catches the interception, which is a defence working rather than the general case.

questions.prompt: Why are social engineering attacks effective against organisations with strong technical controls?

options.text: They target the people authorised to bypass those controls
They exploit vulnerabilities the controls have not been patched against
They arrive over channels that cannot be monitored
They use encryption that security tools cannot inspect

questions.explanation: The attack asks somebody with legitimate access to use it, so no control is defeated technically and nothing looks anomalous. There is no software vulnerability being exploited, which is why patching does not help. Email and telephone are monitorable, and monitoring them does not stop a convincing request. Encryption is not what makes these work, since the persuasion happens in ordinary readable messages.

questions.prompt: Which control most directly limits address flooding on an access port?

options.text: Port security, restricting how many addresses a port may learn
A longer forwarding table ageing time
Spanning tree protection on that port
An access list applied to the switch's management interface

questions.explanation: Limiting the number of addresses learned on a port stops one device filling the table, and the port can be configured to act when the limit is exceeded. A longer ageing time makes the table fill more readily rather than less. Spanning tree protection prevents a device becoming part of the switching topology and does nothing about learned addresses. A management interface access list protects administrative access rather than forwarding behaviour.

questions.prompt: Why does an amplification attack use a third-party service?

options.text: A small request produces a much larger response sent to the victim
The third party's address is harder to block than the attacker's
The third party's traffic is trusted and not inspected
The third party absorbs the return traffic on the attacker's behalf

questions.explanation: The attacker sends small requests with the victim's address as the source, and the service replies with something much larger, so the attacker's own bandwidth is multiplied. Blocking difficulty is a side effect, and the reflection also hides the origin. Trust is not why it works, since the volume rather than the content causes the damage. The third party sends traffic to the victim rather than absorbing anything.

questions.prompt: An access list has a permit rule below a broader deny rule that covers the same traffic. What happens?

options.text: The deny applies, because evaluation stops at the first match
The permit applies, because specific rules outrank general ones
Both are evaluated and the more specific one wins
The list is rejected as contradictory when it is applied

questions.explanation: Evaluation runs top to bottom and stops at the first match, so a rule below one that already matched never runs, which is why order is the most common source of surprises in a list. Specificity ranking is how routing tables work and not how access lists work, and confusing the two is the trap. Nothing evaluates every rule and then compares. Contradictory rules are accepted without complaint, which is why counters are worth having.

questions.prompt: What is the implicit deny at the end of an access list?

options.text: Traffic matching no rule is dropped, whether or not anybody wrote that
A rule automatically added to log unmatched traffic
A default permit applied when a list is empty
A rule that must be written explicitly or the list fails

questions.explanation: Anything not permitted is denied by default, so an incomplete list blocks more than its author intended and a list of permits is a complete policy. It does not log anything, which is why an explicit deny with logging at the end is a common addition. An empty list on most platforms denies rather than permits, which surprises people applying one before finishing it. The rule exists whether or not it is written, which is what implicit means.

questions.prompt: Why is filtering by name harder to enforce than filtering by address?

options.text: A name resolves to addresses that change and differ between clients
Names are not visible to any filtering device
Name filtering requires decrypting all traffic
Names cannot be used in a rule on any platform

questions.explanation: A name may resolve to many addresses, may change without notice, and may resolve differently for different clients, so a rule written against a name is a rule against a moving target. Names are visible in several places including resolution traffic and the server name in a handshake. Decryption helps for some inspection and is not required to see a name in a resolution query. Many platforms do support name-based rules, and how they implement them is exactly where the difficulty shows.

questions.prompt: What does a screened subnet provide?

options.text: A segment for public services with filtering on both sides
A segment where all traffic is encrypted
A segment reserved for network management traffic
A segment with no route to the internet

questions.explanation: Public-facing services sit in a segment with filtering between the internet and it, and between it and the internal network, so a compromise there does not immediately reach everything. Encryption is not what defines it. Management traffic belongs in its own segment for its own reasons and is a different design. A segment with no internet route would be unable to serve the public, which is the opposite of the purpose.

questions.prompt: Which hardening steps close the most exposure for the least effort? (Select two.)

options.text: Changing default credentials
Disabling unused services and management protocols
Enabling every logging option available
Replacing the device with a newer model

questions.explanation: Default credentials are published and are the first thing anything automated tries, and unused services are attack surface that nobody is watching, so both are quick and remove real exposure. Logging everything produces volume that hides the entries worth reading and costs storage, so selective logging is better than maximal. Replacing hardware is expensive and does nothing about the configuration, which is where these weaknesses live.

questions.prompt: Why is port security described as a speed bump rather than a strong control?

options.text: A hardware address can be changed to match one that is permitted
It can only be applied to trunk ports
It stops working once a device has been learned
It requires an authentication server to be effective

questions.explanation: Hardware addresses are trivially changed on most operating systems, so an attacker who can observe a permitted address can present it, which limits the control to accidents and casual misuse. It applies to access ports, which is where devices connect. It continues to enforce after learning, which is what sticky learning is for. It needs no authentication server, and needing one is what distinguishes the stronger control that replaces it.

questions.prompt: What does 802.1X change about how a port behaves?

options.text: The port passes no traffic until the device has authenticated
The port learns only one address and blocks the rest
The port encrypts all traffic it forwards
The port is assigned to a VLAN based on the cable it uses

questions.explanation: The port stays closed to ordinary traffic until an authentication exchange succeeds, so an unauthorised device gets nothing rather than getting access it might misuse. Learning one address is port security, which is the weaker control this replaces. The port does not encrypt traffic, and encryption on wireless comes from the wireless security standard rather than from the authentication framework. VLAN assignment can follow a successful authentication, which is a capability built on top rather than the mechanism.

questions.prompt: Why are building systems and cameras usually placed in their own segment?

options.text: They are rarely patched, so their reach is limited instead
They generate far more traffic than ordinary user devices
They require addresses from a different private range
They cannot coexist with ordinary devices on one switch

questions.explanation: Devices that cannot be updated are managed by controlling what they can reach and what can reach them, since the usual answer of patching is unavailable. Traffic volume is usually modest and is not the reason. Address ranges are a design choice rather than a requirement of the devices. They coexist on a switch perfectly well, which is exactly why a VLAN rather than separate hardware is the usual answer.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum a guest network should do?

options.text: Reach the internet and nothing on the internal network
Require a unique account for every visitor
Log the full browsing history of every guest
Provide the same bandwidth as the internal network

questions.explanation: Separating guests from internal systems while giving them internet access is the whole purpose, and everything else is optional. Unique accounts are useful in some settings and are disproportionate for a waiting room. Logging browsing history raises privacy obligations and is rarely necessary. Bandwidth is a service decision, and guest traffic is often deliberately limited so it does not compete with work.

questions.prompt: Where should the most specific rules go in an access list?

options.text: Near the top, above the broader rules they are exceptions to
Near the bottom, so broad rules are evaluated first
In a separate list applied after the main one
Anywhere, because the most specific rule always wins

questions.explanation: Since evaluation stops at the first match, an exception has to appear before the general rule it modifies or it will never be reached. Putting specific rules last guarantees they are shadowed. A second list changes where the rules live without changing the ordering problem. Specificity does not win in an access list, which is the difference from routing that catches people repeatedly.

questions.prompt: Why is disabling an unused management protocol worthwhile even on an internal network?

options.text: It removes an attack surface nobody is monitoring
It reduces the device's processor load significantly
It is required before the device can be patched
It prevents the device from being discovered by scanning

questions.explanation: A service nobody uses is a service nobody watches, and it will be exploited without anybody noticing it was there, which is why turning it off is worth more than the effort suggests. Processor savings are negligible for a listening service. Patching does not depend on it. The device remains discoverable through whatever it does still run, so hiding is not the benefit.

questions.prompt: A scanner reports that a server runs a version with a published flaw. In the exam's vocabulary, what has the scanner found?

options.text: A vulnerability
An exploit
A threat
A risk

questions.explanation: A vulnerability is the weakness itself, which is what a scanner detects. An exploit is the working code or technique that takes advantage of it. A threat is the actor or event that might do so. Risk combines the likelihood of that happening with what it would cost, which needs information about the business that a scanner does not have.

questions.prompt: A flaw is being used against systems before the vendor has published a fix. What is that called?

options.text: A zero-day
A published vulnerability with a CVE identifier
An insider threat
A denial of service

questions.explanation: A zero-day is a flaw in active use with no fix available, so the defenders have had no days to prepare. A vulnerability with an identifier is one that has been catalogued, which usually means a fix or a workaround exists. An insider threat describes who the actor is rather than the state of the fix. A denial of service is an attack on availability.

questions.prompt: A design assumes any single control will eventually be bypassed and places several independent controls between an attacker and the data. What principle is that?

options.text: Defense in depth
Least privilege
Separation of duties
Implicit deny

questions.explanation: Defense in depth layers controls so that the failure of one does not hand over everything behind it. Least privilege limits what an account may do rather than how many controls sit in the path. Separation of duties splits a sensitive task between people. Implicit deny is the rule at the end of an access list that drops anything unmatched.

questions.prompt: A login requires a password and the answer to a security question. Is that multi-factor authentication?

options.text: No, because both are things the user knows
Yes, because two separate credentials are required
Yes, because the second one is not stored with the first
No, because a security question is not a credential

questions.explanation: A factor is a category, not a count, and a password and a memorised answer are both things the user knows. Two of the same kind is still one factor. Adding something the user has, such as a token or a code from a device, or something the user is, makes it genuinely multi-factor. How the answers are stored does not change which category they fall into.

questions.prompt: An organisation wants administrative commands on network devices authorised individually and the whole exchange encrypted. Which service is designed for that?

options.text: TACACS+
RADIUS
LDAP
Kerberos

questions.explanation: TACACS+ separates authentication from authorisation, so individual commands can be permitted or refused, and it encrypts the entire payload rather than one field. RADIUS combines authentication with authorisation and encrypts only the password. LDAP is a directory protocol that services query rather than a device administration protocol. Kerberos is a ticket-based authentication system used mostly inside a domain.

questions.prompt: A team deploys a system that has no legitimate users and no production role. What is the value of the alerts it produces?

options.text: Any activity on it is unauthorised by definition, so there are no false positives to sift
It absorbs the attacks that would otherwise have reached the production systems
It slows an attacker down for long enough that a response team can be assembled
It records evidence in a form that would be admissible against the attacker

questions.explanation: The value of a honeypot is the quality of its signal: nothing legitimate has any reason to touch it, so a connection is worth investigating without the sifting an ordinary alert needs. It is not sized or positioned to absorb an attack. Slowing an attacker is a side effect at best. Evidence gathering is a legal question rather than the operational reason for deploying one.

questions.prompt: Users at one site are sent to a fraudulent server when they type a legitimate name, and the resolver returns a false address. Which attack is that?

options.text: DNS poisoning
An evil twin
A rogue DHCP server
MAC flooding

questions.explanation: DNS poisoning places a false record where a resolver will serve it, so a correct name returns an attacker's address. An evil twin is a wireless access point impersonating a legitimate network. A rogue DHCP server hands out its own gateway and resolver settings, which can lead somewhere similar but does it by changing the client's configuration rather than the answer. MAC flooding fills a switch's table so it floods traffic.

questions.prompt: An attacker on a segment sends unsolicited replies claiming the gateway's address belongs to their own hardware address. What does that achieve, and why do the victims not notice?

options.text: Traffic for the gateway goes to the attacker, and nothing in the protocol lets a host tell a false reply from a true one
The switch stops forwarding on that segment, and the victims read it as a link failure and call it in
The real gateway is taken offline, and the victims fail over to a second router without noticing
The victims are moved into another VLAN, and nothing on the host reports that it happened

questions.explanation: Address resolution has no authentication, so a host caches whatever answer arrives and sends its gateway traffic to the attacker. Nothing fails, which is why nobody notices. The switch keeps forwarding normally. The real gateway stays up. No VLAN membership changes.

questions.prompt: Which two conditions make VLAN hopping possible on an access port?

options.text: A port that will negotiate trunking, or a native VLAN shared with a user VLAN
A port with port security disabled, or a full forwarding table
A trunk carrying every VLAN, or a missing voice VLAN
A duplicate IP address, or an expired DHCP lease

questions.explanation: A port that negotiates trunking can be talked into becoming one, at which point the attacker reaches every VLAN it carries. A native VLAN shared with a user VLAN lets a doubly tagged frame have its outer tag stripped and be forwarded into another VLAN. Port security and the forwarding table concern flooding rather than tag handling. The last two are addressing faults.

questions.prompt: Staff in a coffee shop connect to a network with the company's SSID and their traffic passes through an attacker. What is the attack?

options.text: An evil twin
A rogue DHCP server
DNS poisoning
A reflection attack

questions.explanation: An evil twin is an access point broadcasting a name clients already trust, so devices associate with it and the operator sits in the path. A rogue DHCP server operates on a network the client is already on. DNS poisoning corrupts name answers rather than the association. A reflection attack bounces traffic off a third party toward a victim.

questions.prompt: What makes a distributed denial of service harder to deal with at the target than a single-source one?

options.text: There is no single source to block, and the volume can exceed the link itself
The traffic is encrypted and cannot be inspected
It targets the application rather than the network
It exploits a vulnerability rather than consuming capacity

questions.explanation: Blocking one source is easy; blocking thousands is not, and once the volume exceeds the circuit's capacity the damage happens upstream of anything the target controls. Encryption is not what defines the attack. Distributed attacks target both networks and applications. Volumetric attacks consume capacity rather than exploiting a flaw, which is why filtering at the target is often too late.

questions.prompt: A wireless network permits only a list of known hardware addresses. Why is that a weak control?

options.text: A hardware address is announced in the clear and can be changed to match a permitted one
Hardware addresses are reassigned every time a device reconnects to the network
The list is held in hardware and cannot hold more than a few hundred entries
Hardware addresses are not visible to the access point until after association

questions.explanation: Every frame carries its source address in the clear, so an attacker watching the air can read a permitted address and set their own interface to match it in seconds. Addresses do not rotate on their own, and randomisation is a privacy feature rather than a defeat of the control. List size is an implementation limit rather than the objection. The access point sees every address, which is how the filter works at all.

questions.prompt: In an 802.1X exchange, which device decides whether the port carries anything beyond the authentication conversation?

options.text: The authenticator, which is the switch port or access point itself
The supplicant, which is the device asking to join the network
The authentication server, which holds the credentials being checked
The certificate authority, which issued the credential being presented

questions.explanation: The authenticator is the switch port or access point standing between the device and the network, passing nothing but the authentication exchange until the server says otherwise. The supplicant is the device asking for access. The authentication server holds the credentials and makes the decision without touching the port. A certificate authority issues certificates and is not one of the three roles.

questions.prompt: Which term does this exam use for a segment holding publicly reachable services with filtering on both sides of it?

options.text: Screened subnet
Demilitarised zone
Trusted zone
Management VLAN

questions.explanation: Screened subnet is the term the objectives use, and the older name for the same arrangement does not appear in them. A trusted zone is the internal side rather than the exposed segment. A management VLAN carries device administration and should not hold public services at all.
